questions.question: Define final consumption expenditure by households (C) and by general government (G), describe the composition of each, and explain the two items that must be kept out of G and where each is actually recorded.
questions.expected_answer: C is spending by households on goods and services that satisfy their wants directly, and it dominates the expenditure side at roughly sixty cents of every rand of domestic spending. It is composed of durable goods lasting three years or more, such as cars, washing machines and laptops; semi-durable goods such as uniforms, shoes and curtains; non-durable goods such as maize meal, petrol, prepaid electricity and medicine; and services such as transport, school fees, data and insurance, which are consumed the moment they are delivered. G is the day-to-day spending of national, provincial and local government on goods and services — salaries of teachers, doctors and traffic officers, plus textbooks, vaccines, diesel and electricity used in delivering public services. Two items must be evicted from G. Transfer payments such as social grants and bursaries are excluded because government receives no good or service in return; the money is recorded once, inside C, when the receiving household spends it, and putting it in G as well would count the same rand twice. Government capital expenditure — a new library, water treatment works or rail line — is also excluded because it creates an asset rather than consuming anything, so it is recorded under gross fixed capital formation, I.

questions.question: Define gross fixed capital formation, list its composition and the institutions that carry it out, calculate net investment from the lesson's figures, and explain why this component matters more for future growth than C or G.
questions.expected_answer: Gross fixed capital formation is spending on fixed capital — assets that serve in production repeatedly for longer than a year. It includes dwellings and other buildings; construction works such as highways, railways, dams, harbours and transmission lines; machinery and equipment; production vehicles; computers, software and networks; and cultivated biological assets such as orchards, vines and dairy herds. Buying an existing asset is excluded because the nation's stock of assets is unchanged — only the owner changed — and the change in inventories is capital formation but not fixed, so it is shown on a separate line. Investment is carried out by private business enterprises, which do the largest share, by public corporations running electricity, rail, port and water infrastructure, and by general government. With gross investment of R1 000 billion and consumption of fixed capital of R620 billion, net investment is R380 billion; only that portion enlarges capacity, and an economy investing less than its depreciation is eating its own machines. Investment matters most because it expands productive capacity — the outward shift of the production possibility curve — raises productivity by equipping workers with better tools, creates jobs in both building and operating the assets, and lowers costs for every user. At R1 000 billion against GDP of R6 700 billion the ratio is about 14,9 per cent, less than half of the roughly 30 per cent of GDP the National Development Plan targets.

questions.question: Using the lesson's figures, run the chain from GNE to GDP to GVA and to GNI, stating what each conversion corrects for and why South Africa's GNI sits below its GDP.
questions.expected_answer: GNE is C of 4 200 plus G of 1 500 plus I of 1 000 minus 60 for the rundown of inventories, giving R6 640 billion — total spending by residents on final goods and services, also published as GDE. The trade conversion adds exports of 2 100 and subtracts imports of 2 040, so GDP at market prices is R6 700 billion; this corrects for the fact that some resident spending bought foreign output while foreigners bought some of ours, and this year production exceeded residents' spending by 60 billion, which left as net exports. The price-tag conversion links GDP to GVA at basic prices: GVA of 6 000 plus taxes on products of 730 minus subsidies of 30 equals 6 700, so the conversion only changes the price at which the same output is valued — the producer's price versus the shelf price. The ownership conversion turns domestic into national: add primary income received from abroad of 110 and subtract primary income paid abroad of 290, giving GNI of R6 520 billion. South Africa's GNI sits below its GDP because a meaningful share of the profit and interest generated inside the country is owed to foreign owners of the capital that built mines, malls and cell towers here, so net primary income of R180 billion flows out.
